complexity.explanation: Linear search scans each element sequentially until the target is found. Best case occurs when the target is at the first position. Average case examines half the elements. Worst case examines all elements. Space complexity is O(1) as it uses only a few variables.

description.brief: A simple searching algorithm that sequentially checks each element in the array until the target is found or the array ends.
detailed: Algorithm Analysis:
Time Complexity:
• Best case:    O(1)   - target found at first position
• Average case: O(n/2) ≈ O(n) - examines half the elements
• Worst case:   O(n)   - target not found or at last position
Space Complexity: O(1) - uses constant extra space
Key Characteristics:
• Works on both sorted and unsorted arrays
• Extremely simple to implement
• Excellent for small datasets (< 100 elements)
• No preprocessing required
• Adaptive: can stop immediately when target found
Performance Metrics:
• Comparisons: Up to n in worst case
• Memory: Constant O(1) auxiliary space
• Best for: Unsorted data, small arrays, single searches
Comparison with Other Search Algorithms:
• Binary Search: O(log n) but requires sorted data
• Sentinel Search: Slightly faster by removing boundary check
• Index Search: Uses index table for faster searching
• Hash Table: O(1) average but requires hash function

return i;   // Target found at index i
optimizations: Sentinel linear search (removes boundary check at cost of extra memory)
Parallel linear search for multi-core processors
Bloom filter pre-filtering for negative searches
use_cases: Real-time systems where O(n) is acceptable
Finding first occurrence of an element
When data is streamed or generated on-the-fly
disadvantages: Slow for large datasets (O(n) worst case)
Inefficient for multiple searches on same data
Poor performance compared to hash-based methods
Not suitable for production systems with large data
Does not use array ordering to optimize
